object_entity.proposition_label: Post-baptismal sin can be forgiven through penance
object_entity.description: A second repentance after baptism is possible and administered through church discipline.

context_place.notes: Imperial capital associated with the Roman church and Paul later ministry.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Callistus alleged that the parable of the tares growing together with the wheat was spoken in reference to the Church: sinners should remain in the Church. He also affirmed that the ark of Noah was a figure of the Church, in which were dogs, hawks, and other unclean animals — so must the Church tolerate sinners.
passage.notes: Callistus defends leniency toward sinners using parables of tares and Noah's ark; penitential controversy

object_entity.proposition_label: The rule of faith is received from the apostles
object_entity.description: Christians hold to a received standard of teaching traced to the apostles and guarded by their successors.

context_place.notes: Imperial capital associated with the Roman church and Paul later ministry.

evidence.notes: Hippolytus appeals to received tradition against Callistus's innovations.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Callistus, having been appointed over the cemetery by Zephyrinus, brought many into his following. He was the first to invent the device of conniving at the sensual pleasures of men, saying that all men had their sins forgiven by himself. For he even permitted women of rank, if they were unmarried and burned with lust, to have a companion of the rank of slave or freedman.
passage.notes: Hippolytus attacks Callistus for moral laxity; permitting marriages between social classes; forgiving grave sins

object_entity.proposition_label: The Son is eternally begotten from the Father
object_entity.description: The Son/Logos is not a creature brought into being at a point in time but is eternally generated from the substance of the Father — there was never a time when the Son was not. Key Origenian contribution that became foundational for Nicene orthodoxy.

context_place.notes: Major Egyptian port city; intellectual and commercial center; seat of the Catechetical School; major Christian center from the first century onward.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Eusebius preserves a letter of Cornelius of Rome describing Novatian's ordination irregularity: three simple and rustic bishops from Italy were brought to Rome and compelled to lay hands on Novatian by a counterfeit and vain laying on of hands; Novatian seized the bishopric by craft and treachery. Cornelius also lists the Roman clergy: forty-six presbyters, seven deacons, seven subdeacons, forty-two acolytes, and fifty-two exorcists, readers, and doorkeepers. More than fifteen hundred widows and distressed persons are supported by the Lord's grace and kindness.
passage.notes: Cornelius on Novatian's irregular ordination; Roman church size and clerical orders c. 251

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Theophilus called the Indian was sent by Emperor Constantius on an embassy to the Himyarites in south Arabia. He was originally from the island of Dibus (Socotra). He converted the Himyarites and built three churches: one in Zafar the capital, one in Aden, and one near the Persian Gulf. He also visited the Aksumites and corrected their worship.
passage.notes: Key source for Arabian/Himyarite Christianity and Theophilus's mission; preserved in Photius's epitome.

object_entity.proposition_label: The apostle Bartholomew preached in India and left a Hebrew Gospel of Matthew
object_entity.description: Eusebius HE 5.10 reports that Pantaenus found in India Christians who possessed a Hebrew Matthew left by the apostle Bartholomew; Philostorgius HE 3.6 also mentions Bartholomew.

context_place.notes: Malabar coast of southwest India; traditional site of the Thomas Christians; Pantaenus reportedly found Christians using Matthew's Gospel here (Eusebius HE 5.10).

evidence.notes: Passage contextualizes bartholomew's position on bartholomew-preached-in-india.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: A philosopher named Meropius of Tyre sailed to India with two boys Frumentius and Aedesius. The ship was seized and all killed except the boys who were brought to the king of Aksum. When the king died the queen asked Frumentius to help govern. Frumentius sought out Roman traders who were Christians and built churches. Later he traveled to Alexandria where Athanasius consecrated him bishop. He returned to Aksum and converted many including the king.
passage.notes: Primary Western source for the christianization of Aksum; Rufinus heard the account from Aedesius himself.
